summary: Describes the ATM call control signaling exchanges needed to support Classical IP over ATM, as described in RFC 1577. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: ATM networks set up a connection before data can flow, and the connection is described in a message full of options. This RFC says which of those options an IP router or host has to fill in, so that two different implementations can talk to each other.

questions: what is atm signaling for ip
how does classical ip over atm set up a connection
what is the default ip mtu over atm aal5
subtitle: How an IP host or router should fill in ATM call setup messages so Classical IP over ATM interoperates.

tldr.problem: Classical IP over ATM and its encapsulation need ATM connections to be set up on demand, but ATM signalling offers many options and there was no single agreed way to use them for IP.
tldr.mechanism: This implementors guide says which signalling messages and information elements an IP-over-ATM endsystem must send in a SETUP, how to code them for AAL 5 and LLC/SNAP, how to manage and tear down several connections, and how to react when a call fails.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard written against ATM Forum UNI 3.1, with appendices for UNI 3.0 and Frame Relay interworking. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 1755 is a Proposed Standard published in February 1995. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is written against the ATM Forum UNI 3.1 signalling, and the RFC notes that future revisions may use ATM capabilities that were not yet available.

sections.title: What ATM Signaling Does for IP
sections.content:
In a switched virtual connection environment, ATM virtual channel connections are established and released as they are needed. The ATM call and connection control signalling protocol, which runs between the ATM endsystems and the ATM network, does this. The signalling establishes and releases calls, which are the association between ATM endpoints, and the connections themselves. It uses addressing to locate ATM endpoints and to allocate resources in the network for the connection, and it lets the two endpoints negotiate and select the end-to-end protocols and their parameters.

This memo describes how that signalling protocol is used to support IP over ATM, and in particular which information is exchanged to make it work. The resolution of IP addresses to ATM addresses and the routing questions are not in scope here; they belong to RFC 1577.

The specification is written against the ATM Forum User-Network Interface specification version 3.1, which the ATM Forum produced largely to align with ITU-T Recommendation Q.2931. UNI 3.1 is based on UNI 3.0 but the two versions are incompatible, and Appendix B of the RFC explains how to support IP over ATM with UNI 3.0 signalling instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Before an ATM network can carry IP traffic, it has to set up a connection and agree on what kind of traffic it will be. This RFC is the agreed way to make that agreement, so that any two ATM systems set up the same connection in the same way.

sections.title: Opening, Sharing and Closing Connections
sections.content:
The owner of a connection is the entity inside the ATM endsystem that established it. An endsystem may establish a call when it has a datagram to send and either there is no existing connection it can use, it chooses not to use one, for instance for route optimization or quality of service, or the owner does not allow sharing.

To keep the address resolution at the called station fast, the calling endstation may send an InARP_REQUEST after the connection is established and before it sends its first data packet, and it may send data without waiting for the reply. A called endstation may tie the calling party number from the SETUP message to the connection, so that later traffic to the same ATM address can use it.

One connection may carry several protocols when the owner allows sharing and the encapsulation can multiplex them, which LLC/SNAP can. The system must then watch the traffic at the lowest multiplexing layer to notice when the connection is idle. Systems must be able to support several connections between peers, and if a receiver accepts more than one call from one source it must then accept traffic on the additional connections. Because several connections are allowed, the collision-handling algorithms of ISO/IEC 8473 must not be used. If a system is configured to allow only one connection to a destination and a colliding call arrives, the incoming call must be rejected, and each system must wait at least a configurable collision retry time in the range of 1 to 10 seconds, with a random increment and exponential backoff.

Either end may close a connection, and a datagram in flight when the connection closes or is reset is lost. Systems should be able to configure a minimum holding time, with 60 seconds suggested as the default, and any system with a public UNI interface must support a configurable inactivity timer, with 20 minutes recommended as the default, which must watch traffic in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules here stop two systems from opening a pile of connections to each other. A connection can be shared by several protocols, it should stay open for a minimum time, and an idle one should be cleaned up after a while.

sections.title: Call Setup and Release Messages
sections.content:
The point-to-point signalling messages are SETUP, CALL PROCEEDING, CONNECT and CONNECT ACKNOWLEDGE for call setup, and RELEASE and RELEASE COMPLETE for call release. An ATM endpoint starts a call by sending SETUP to the network. The network works out whether the call can go ahead, and if it can, it returns the newly allocated VPCI and VCI in its first response, which is either a CALL PROCEEDING or a CONNECT message. If the call cannot be accepted, by the network or by the destination, a RELEASE COMPLETE is sent. At the destination, the network offers the call with a SETUP message; the destination answers CONNECT, which may be preceded by CALL PROCEEDING, or refuses with RELEASE COMPLETE.

Either endpoint, and rarely the network, can start the release. An endpoint that wants to release a call sends RELEASE, the network answers RELEASE COMPLETE, frees the resources of the call and starts clearing towards the other endpoint. The network starts clearing by sending RELEASE to the far endpoint, which answers with RELEASE COMPLETE, and the network then frees the resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up a call is four messages: a request, an acknowledgement, a connect, and a confirmation. Tearing it down is two: a release and a release complete.

sections.title: What a SETUP Message Must Contain
sections.content:
A signalling message holds mandatory and optional variable-length information elements, which are further split into octet groups and fields. The information elements carry what is relevant to the network, to the peer endpoint, or to both, and the choice of optional elements and their contents decides who the parties are and what the connection will carry. A call for constant bitrate video over AAL 1 therefore has different contents from a call for IP over AAL 5.

A SETUP message that establishes a connection for IP and multiprotocol interconnection must contain the AAL Parameters, the ATM Traffic Descriptor, the Broadband Bearer Capability, the Broadband Low Layer Information, the QoS Parameter, the Called Party Number and the Calling Party Number. It may also contain the Calling Party Subaddress, the Called Party Subaddress and the Transit Network Selection.

In UNI 3.1 the AAL Parameters and the Broadband Low Layer Information elements are optional in a SETUP message, but for IP over ATM both must be included. Appendix A of the RFC shows a sample SETUP message coded in that way.
sections.plainLanguage: A SETUP message for IP has to carry seven pieces of information, and two of them are optional in the ordinary ATM specification but mandatory here, because they say how the IP traffic is carried.

sections.title: Adaptation Layer and Encapsulation Settings
sections.content:
The AAL Parameters element says which ATM Adaptation Layer the connection uses. Since RFC 1483 specifies IP over AAL 5, the AAL type field must say AAL 5. The forward and backward maximum CPCS-SDU size fields carry the desired IP MTU; their values range from zero to 65,535, and although the default IP MTU over AAL 5 is 9188 bytes, endstations are encouraged to support MTU sizes up to and including 64k. No Service Specific Convergence Sublayer is normally used for multiprotocol interconnection over AAL 5, so the SSCS type field should be absent, or coded as the null SSCS.

The Broadband Low Layer Information element, together with the AAL Parameters element and the B-LLI negotiation procedure, is how the encapsulation is chosen. RFC 1577 specifies LLC/SNAP as the default encapsulation, and it must be implemented by all endstations. The element has a layer 2 identifier of 2 and a user information layer of 12, which is lan_llc from ISO 8802/2. Only LLC is indicated, because it is the LLC layer's job to look at the encapsulation header of the packets that follow and hand the ones marked as IP up to IP.

A B-LLI may also carry a layer 3 identifier of 3 with the ISO/IEC TR 9577 protocol codepoint, to say that IP will manage the call and that the connection will carry only IP traffic. Called parties must accept that form of call setup, and the caller must still use LLC/SNAP encapsulation on all its IP datagrams, because the receiver may still choose to multiplex the call through LLC.
sections.plainLanguage: Two elements decide how the IP packets are carried: the adaptation layer, which must be AAL 5, and the encapsulation, which is LLC/SNAP by default. The same header is used on every packet so that the far end can tell which packets are IP.

sections.title: Traffic, Bearer, QoS and Address Elements
sections.content:
The ATM Traffic Descriptor describes the connection by its peak cell rate, sustainable cell rate and maximum burst size, which is what the network uses to allocate bandwidth and buffers. The model that best matches how IP behaves is the Best Effort capability, which may be requested by including the best effort indication together with the forward and backward peak cell rates. When it is used, the network gives no guarantees at all and the throughput may even be zero at any time.

When Best Effort is not used, or when a more predictable service is wanted, more specific parameters may be given. The RFC presents the subset of traffic management that every IP over ATM endsystem must support, in three combinations: a token bucket style description for a source that sends in bursts, a description intended for ATM pipes such as the link between two routers, and the best effort combination. All of them use QoS class 0, the unspecified class, which is the only class every network must support and the only one allowed with best effort service. There is no negotiation of the traffic descriptor, the bearer capability or the QoS parameters in the UNI specification, so the calling endsystem is expected to know in advance what both ends and the network will accept, and to retry the call with different values when it is refused for those reasons.

ATM addressing information travels in the Called Party Number, Calling Party Number and, in some circumstances, the subaddress elements. A router that supports several logical IP subnets on one physical ATM interface may give them different ATM addresses that differ only in the Selector field, which can tell up to 256 such subnets apart for the same end system identifier, and its signalling entity must then carry the right addresses in the calling and called party number elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The traffic descriptor says how much traffic the connection should carry and with what guarantees. Best effort asks for no guarantees at all, which is the closest match to how IP normally behaves. There is no negotiation, so the two ends have to agree in advance.

sections.title: When a Call Fails
sections.content:
When a call attempt fails for one of a set of causes, the situation should be treated as Network Unreachable if the called endsystem is a router, or as Host Unreachable if it is a host, following the treatment of those conditions in RFC 1122. The causes are: unallocated number, no route to destination, user busy, no user responding, destination out of order, network out of order, temporary failure, and resource unavailable unspecified.

For a different set of causes the endsystem may retry the call, changing or adding the elements the cause code points at. These are: no route to specified transit network, call rejected, number changed, user rejects call with calling line identification restriction, user cell rate unavailable, quality of service unavailable, bearer capability not authorized, bearer capability not presently available, bearer capability not implemented, unsupported combination of traffic parameters, incompatible destination, invalid transmit network selection, and AAL parameter cannot be supported. Appendix A of the RFC shows the sample signalling messages, and Appendix C lists the combinations of traffic related parameters that are allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some failures mean the far end is unreachable and there is no point retrying. Others are about the connection setup itself, and the system can try again with different settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is brief here, and says why: not all of the security issues that relate to IP over ATM were clearly understood at the time, because the ATM specifications were still moving and the technology was new. It says that future revisions will address the security capabilities that future signalling standards may offer to IP over ATM signalling.

Two other points are worth noting. The IP address to ATM address resolution is out of scope of this memo, and is treated in RFC 1577 instead, and the RFC notes that the security of the signalling itself depends on the signalling standards that were still being written.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not say much about security. It explains that the ATM specifications were still changing when it was written, and that a later version would cover whatever security the signalling standards ended up offering.
